book.subject: cte

title: Poultry production and its types
competency: Explain why poultry matters and compare the four production systems.

keywords.def: Raising chickens for meat, eggs and feathers.
Chickens are not confined and search for food over a wide area.
Chickens are fully confined in houses or cages and fed by the owner.

en.text: Almost every rural family owns chickens. Poultry is the smallest livestock investment, and gives protein and income: eggs give small regular income, live birds give cash when needed. Poultry can help fight poverty and improve nutrition and food security.

screens.title: Brainstorming
screens.ask: List the activities in producing a chicken from an egg. What comes first?
opts: Selecting a good hen and good eggs
screens.after: It starts with good hens and eggs, then hatching, feeding, housing and care.

screens.title: 3.4.1 Introduction
paras: Almost every rural family owns chickens.
They give protein and income to the family.
Poultry is the smallest livestock investment a household can make.

screens.title: Income and food
paras: Eggs give a regular, small income.
Selling live birds gives cash when it is needed.
Poultry is part of most Ethiopian households: rural, urban and semi-urban.
Poultry can help with poverty alleviation, nutrition and food security.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Raising chickens for meat, eggs and feathers.

screens.text: Poultry can play a key role in:
Poultry is the smallest livestock investment a village household can make.
What does selling eggs usually give a family?
screens.why: Eggs give regular income; live birds give flexible cash.

screens.text: Meron's family needs money for school fees next month. Which poultry product gives cash when needed?
screens.why: Live birds are a flexible source of cash when needed. Eggs give small, regular income.

en.text: There are four systems. Free-range: chickens are not confined and scavenge widely. Backyard: housed at night, free during the day, with a little grain. Semi-intensive: confined to a fenced area with shelter. Intensive: fully confined in houses or cages, with higher cost, and birds depend on the owner for everything.

screens.title: Which system?
screens.ask: Chickens sleep in a shelter at night and walk around the compound by day. Which system is this?
screens.after: Housed at night, free by day: the backyard system.

screens.title: 3.4.2 Types of poultry production
paras: There are four systems in Ethiopia and Africa.
table: Not confined; search for food widely; may nest in the bush
Housed at night; free by day; a handful of grain
Confined to a fenced area with shelter
Fully confined in houses or cages

screens.title: Traditional production
paras: Intensive systems cost more. The birds depend on the owner for all needs.
The traditional system makes the best use of local resources.
Chickens breed fast and their products are easy to sell.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Chickens are not confined and search for food over a wide area.
Chickens are fully confined in houses or cages and fed by the owner.

screens.text: In which system are chickens fully confined in houses or cages?

screens.why: Confinement increases from free-range to intensive.
screens.clue: How freely can the birds move?

screens.text: Under free-range conditions, chickens can scavenge for food over a wide area.

screens.title: Order from least confined to most confined
screens.why: From least to most confined, and from lowest to highest cost.
screens.clue: Start with the most free system.

items.text: What is the main difference between the four poultry systems?
opts: How freely the chickens can move (confinement)
The number of eggs per day
items.ans: How freely the chickens can move (confinement)
items.why: From not confined to fully confined; cost rises too.

test.text: How many poultry production systems does the book describe?
Almost every rural family owns chickens.
Which system has the highest capital outlay?
test.why: Birds depend fully on the owner.

test.text: In the semi-intensive system, chickens nest in the bush.
test.why: That is free-range; semi-intensive birds stay in a fenced area.
